question: During the hearing before the Committee on Economic Affairs on 10 September 2026 in Parliament, the Commission stated that further European integration of banking supervision is necessary to facilitate cross-border banking activities and to complete the Banking Union. At the same time, it acknowledged that Member States are concerned about the implications of greater flexibility regarding the holding of capital and liquidity outside the home Member State. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that further European integration of banking supervision and greater flexibility regarding cross-border capital and liquidity flows do not result in national taxpayers ultimately bearing the financial risks of banking activities carried out elsewhere in the Union?

What specific safeguards will the Commission put in place to ensure that the principle of risk-sharing within the Banking Union is accompanied by a proportionate allocation of responsibility and liability for those risks, including within a bank or banking group?
How does the Commission view the further development and supervision of the interdependence between banks and states in the case of larger, cross-border banks?
answer: The communication of 17 July 2026 (1), on the competitiveness of the banking sector and the Single Market in Banking lays out the Commission’s way forward to reduce various prudential and non-prudential barriers to integration, accompanied by appropriate safeguards ensuring financial stability across the EU.

Proposed safeguards include a review of the structure of the deposit insurance in the Banking Union to ensure that national deposit guarantee schemes (DGSs) would not be affected by the failure of subsidiaries; improving the predictability of group resolution strategies and ensuring that group-wide supervisors have the power to require that the parent allocates sufficient resources to its subsidiaries, including in crises situations.

Finally, any measures to allow cross-border groups to better allocate capital and liquidity should consider the diversity of crossborder banking groups, including the level of integration and commitments made within a group.

The safeguards address the remaining vulnerabilities of DGSs to liquidity shortfalls and contribute to further mitigating the feedback loop between banks and sovereigns, which is less of a concern today than a decade ago.

The safeguards are also intended to provide assurance that in times of crisis, Member States would not be left alone in managing problems faced by subsidiaries of cross-border banking groups without sufficient support, including support from the parent.
